note: The Roman emperor Antoninus told Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi he wanted two things: for his son Asveirus to rule after him, and for Tiberias to be freed from taxes. The Roman leaders would grant one request but not two. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi set one man on another's shoulders, gave a dove to the one on top, and told the one below to tell him to let it fly. Antoninus understood: ask for his son to rule, and have his son free Tiberias. When Antoninus complained that important Romans were troubling him, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi took him to his garden and each day pulled up one radish in front of him. Antoninus understood: kill them one by one, and do not provoke them all at once.
why: The Gemara has said that the Romans do sometimes make a king's son king at the king's request, giving Asveirus son of Antoninus as the example. This story shows how that came about. Afterward the Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not simply speak openly.

people.name: Antoninus
people.about: A Roman emperor who seeks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's advice.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; answers Antoninus with silent demonstrations.

people.name: Asveirus
people.about: Antoninus' son, whom he wants to succeed him.

terms.meaning: A city in the Land of Israel.
Antoninus wants Tiberias exempted from paying taxes to Rome.

note: A Roman emperor who hated the Jews asked his nobles whether a man with a sore on his foot should cut it off and live, or leave it and suffer. They said cut it off. Ketia son of Shalom objected: the Jews can never all be destroyed, and Rome would be called the severed kingdom. The emperor agreed but said whoever defeats the king in argument is thrown into a furnace. As Ketia was led away, a noblewoman said: woe to the ship that sails without paying its tax. He circumcised himself and said he had paid his tax. As he was thrown in, he left all his property to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues. A Divine Voice declared Ketia destined for the World-to-Come, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi wept: some earn their world in one moment, others over many years.
why: A teaching reads the verse placing Edom's leaders in the netherworld as not including all its officers; the exception is Ketia son of Shalom. The Gemara asks who he was, and this story answers.

people.name: Ketia son of Shalom
people.about: A Roman official who argues against destroying the Jews and is put to death.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Receives Ketia's property with his colleagues and teaches how to divide it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; weeps when he hears the Divine Voice.

terms.meaning: Here a figure of speech for the Jewish people, whom the emperor wanted to remove.
A place of execution where a person was thrown to die.
A voice from Heaven announcing God's view.
The life after death promised to the righteous.

note: A woman came to Rav Hisda to confess. She said the lightest of her sins was that she had conceived her younger son with her older son. Rav Hisda said to prepare her burial shrouds, but she did not die.
why: The Gemara has read a verse in Proverbs as saying that people who turn back from heresy die. It asks whether that is always so, and brings this woman, whose worst sins implied heresy, as a case where it did not happen; she had not truly repented, it answers.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage to whom the woman confesses.

terms.meaning: The cloth garments a dead body is wrapped in; Rav Hisda is saying she will soon die.
Here, turning away from Jewish belief; the Gemara infers she had done this as well.

note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Arza and Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai were sitting and drinking wine when a man came by, and they asked him to pour for them. After he poured, it turned out he was a gentile. One of the two Sages forbade the wine even for any benefit, while the other allowed it even for drinking. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said both were right: one assumed the gentile thought such great Sages must be drinking wine and might have poured it to an idol, the other that he assumed they were drinking liquor, since they would never ask a gentile to serve them wine.
why: The Gemara has been debating how strictly to treat wine a gentile touched by accident, after Abaye refuted Rava's lenient view; this incident adds a case where the gentile's own assumptions decide whether he meant to offer it to an idol.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Arza
people.about: One of the two Sages drinking wine; one of them forbade it and one permitted it.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai
people.about: The other Sage drinking wine with Rabbi Yohanan ben Arza.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: A Sage who later judged that both rulings were proper and explained each one.

terms.meaning: Offering wine to an idol by pouring it out. Wine a gentile may have poured for an idol was forbidden to Jews, even for selling.
Any use or profit from something, such as selling it, not only eating or drinking it.
